analysis.one_liner: Restricts warrantless government spying on Americans' communications and requires warrants for surveillance.
analysis.headline: The Government Surveillance Reform Act was introduced in November 2023 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it died without a hearing or vote when Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require government agencies to get a warrant before searching surveillance data collected on Americans without one, ban 'backdoor searches' of intelligence databases for information about people in the US, end warrantless collection of domestic communications, require court approval for spying powers currently exercised in secret, and let people challenge unlawful surveillance in court despite the state secrets privilege. It also extends Section 702, the core foreign spying authority, for four more years — trading continued surveillance of foreigners for new protections for Americans.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday Americans whose phone calls, emails, web browsing, location, and car data would get warrant protection before federal agencies search or seize them; it also gives privacy advocates a seat at the secret surveillance court's table and lets victims of illegal spying sue. Tech companies ordered to help spy would get court-checked limits on those demands.

how_it_helps.text: Requires warrants before FBI or other agencies search intelligence databases for communications of or about Americans or anyone in the US, closing the 'backdoor search loophole' in Section 702 of FISA.
Extends similar warrant rules to surveillance under Executive Order 12333 and prohibits intelligence agencies from acquiring Americans' data and domestic communications without a warrant.
Limits how surveillance-derived evidence about Americans can be used in criminal, civil, and administrative proceedings unless it relates to specific national-security threats.

Bans law enforcement from buying Americans' personal data from data brokers without a warrant and requires warrants for location, web browsing, and search records — closing workarounds agencies use to buy data they couldn't legally collect.

Expands the secret surveillance court's independent advisors, requires declassification of significant court rulings, lets those advisors appeal decisions up to the Supreme Court, and ends the state secrets privilege blocking lawsuits over surveillance — meaning Americans could actually challenge illegal spying in court.

Ends 'abouts' collection (sweeping up communications merely mentioning surveillance targets), bans 'reverse targeting' of Americans, imposes five-year data-retention limits, and requires accountability procedures — including possible termination — for federal employees who misuse Americans' data.

analysis.who_pays: Intelligence and law-enforcement agencies (FBI, CIA, NSA, NCTC) and federal prosecutors would lose the ability to search Americans' communications without a judge's sign-off, and would face new reporting, audit, and accountability requirements; telecom and tech providers would face court-supervised limits on compliance demands but also clearer rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: Intelligence agencies and federal law enforcement

drawbacks.text: Replaces the open-ended warrantless-search status quo with a four-year extension of Section 702, so critics on both sides see it as a compromise: surveillance hawks lose unconstrained backdoor searches, while civil libertarians object that bulk collection of foreigners' communications continues and the sunset keeps the program alive.

Emergency and consent exceptions mean warrantless queries are still permitted in narrow circumstances (imminent threat of death or serious bodily harm, consent, defensive cybersecurity), so the bill does not eliminate all warrantless searches of Americans.

Implementation delays, DOJ reporting requirements, and new accountability procedures would add compliance costs and administrative burden for intelligence agencies, and some fear warrants would slow time-sensitive counterterrorism and counterintelligence work.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades a real loss of agency flexibility — no more warrantless searches of Americans' data and data-broker workarounds — for transparency, court oversight, and legal recourse that don't currently exist. The costs fall mostly on government agencies' convenience and speed rather than on ordinary people, though critics argue warrant requirements could impede urgent investigations and that extending Section 702 perpetuates mass collection rather than ending it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on November 7, 2023 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up; it died there when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: The Government Surveillance Reform Act of 2023 was introduced by Sen. Ron Wyden on November 7, 2023, with ten Senate cosponsors split between both parties (7 Democrats, 3 Republicans).
Its only action was referral to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced; no hearing, markup, or floor vote was ever scheduled.
The bill was reintroduced as legislation in the 119th Congress (as H.R. 1475 / S. 663, the same Government Surveillance Reform Act) after this one expired, but the original bill never became law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Intelligence agencies and the FBI benefit from the bill's failure: they keep the ability to search Americans' communications without warrants and to buy personal data from brokers, and face no new accountability for misuse. Privacy advocates and ordinary Americans gained nothing from the effort in this Congress.

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Government Surveillance Reform Act and recruited a bipartisan coalition of cosponsors.

for.name: Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship.

for.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup before Congress ended.

against.name: Intelligence and law-enforcement community
against.role: FBI, NSA, CIA, and DOJ national-security divisions
against.what_they_did: The bill targets the warrantless search and data-broker practices these agencies use; the bill's provisions restricting their authorities and adding accountability procedures were the changes they would most directly resist, and the bill never advanced past referral.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor or prioritized it for a vote during the two years it sat in committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's ten cosponsors split roughly two-to-one Democratic (7 of 48 Senate D, 3 of 49 Senate R), showing bipartisan but modest support; opposition is inferred from inaction rather than any recorded vote, so a party split on merits can't be established from the record.

industries.note: Providers would face court-supervised limits on government demands for technical assistance and clearer minimization rules for voluntarily disclosing customer data, giving them legal clarity while restricting some cooperation with federal agencies.
Law enforcement would be barred from buying Americans' personal location and other data from brokers without a warrant, closing a market these firms currently serve with government customers.

industries.industry: Intelligence community contractors and surveillance-technology vendors
industries.note: Cell site simulators, high-intensity drug-trafficking surveillance programs, and data-retention practices would face new restrictions, independent oversight, and public reporting, shrinking the market for these tools and services.
